# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from it, in its over-center position, the pipe 90 clamped; the lever attitude is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, each seen only radially inside the inner circle of that body, which runs unbroken past them, and each reaching inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10, the others on the second frame half 12; shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
22	
23	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
24	
25	The jaw carriages
26	
27	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.
28	
29	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
30	
31	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
32	
33	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
34	
35	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
36	
37	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
38	
39	The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
40	
41	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.
42	
43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
44	
45	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
46	
47	The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
52	
53	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
54	
55	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.
58

Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

content.text:
The two reviewer findings were both real, and both fixes stayed inside the figure briefs. No application text, claim, or numeral definition changed.

**FIG. 6** (and its echo in **FIG. 4**) had described a joint the inventor never disclosed: a recess in each frame end face, an unhatched segment end *projecting out of* that recess, and the two segment ends meeting midway across a standing gap between frame halves that never touch. That is a load path and a topology, not a depiction convention: it would have put each cam ring segment end outside its own frame half's annular guide, contradicting the description's statement that "the annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10". FIG. 6 now shows the annular guide 18 of each half as a channel opening toward the parting line, with each segment lying in its channel and reaching the end face without passing beyond it, the two end faces meeting at the parting line. Numeral 18 was added to that sheet (6 numerals, within the 8 limit), which also removes the second unnumbered name ("recess") for a structure that already has one. FIG. 4 now says the bodies meet at a parting line, and "the gap width" is gone from its schematic list.

**FIG. 1** had confined each jaw carriage to the region radially inside an inner circle drawn "unbroken past them", which renders three carriages floating free of the frame, and the same sentence also said the topmost one "lies on the first frame half 10". The brief now interrupts the inner circle with a radial opening at each of the three positions, with the carriage's outer portion inside the body and only its inner end standing radially inside that circle, which is what the description and FIG. 3 require and what the 3-3 cutting plane into FIG. 3 must agree with.

Drawing pixels were not inspected or generated here; the briefs are the specification the regeneration runs from.

input.summary: Fixed both reviewer findings, entirely within the figure briefs. FIG. 6 no longer depicts an undisclosed joint (recess plus segment ends projecting into and meeting across a standing gap between frame halves); it now shows each cam ring segment lying in the annular guide 18 of its own frame half and reaching its end face, the two end faces meeting at the parting line, which matches the disclosure ("complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments" when the halves close) and the description's statement that the annular guide retains each segment on its own half. FIG. 4's echo of the gap was corrected the same way and "the gap width" was dropped from its schematic list. FIG. 1 no longer draws the jaw carriages inside an unbroken inner circle detached from the frame; the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening at each of the three positions, with the carriage's outer portion inside the body and its inner end standing radially inside that circle, agreeing with the description, with FIG. 3, and with the 3-3 cutting plane FIG. 1 carries. Application text, claims, and the numeral table are unchanged except that numeral 18, already defined and already used in the text and in FIG. 3, is now listed on FIG. 6 where it is shown.
reasoning: The FIG. 6 finding is correct and was not a depiction-convention question. A recess in the frame end face, a segment end projecting out of it, and the two segment ends meeting midway across a gap between frame halves that never touch, together assert contact, load path, and relative location: that the ring ends rather than the frame are the members in contact, and that each segment end stands outside its own half's annular guide. The disclosure says only that closure couples the segments through faces at the two ends, and the description says the annular guide retains each segment on its own frame half. So I removed the projection and the gap rather than adding text to support them, per the rule that drawings follow the invention.

I used the annular guide, a part the disclosure already gives ('a segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame'), as the structure that holds each segment end in FIG. 6. That closes the second half of the same defect: the sheet had been naming the guide's end a 'recess' with no numeral, so one structure carried two names across the figure set. Numeral 18 now appears on FIG. 6 with a target on the channel wall, bringing that sheet to six numerals, inside the eight-per-sheet limit, and no new part or numeral was created.

The FIG. 1 finding is also correct, and it was self-contradictory as written: the same sentence put each carriage wholly inside the frame's inner circle, told the renderer to run that circle unbroken past them, and said the topmost carriage lies on the first frame half. FIG. 3 requires the radial guide 38 to open at the frame's radially inner surface with only the carriage's inner end projecting past it, so the inner circle cannot be continuous at a carriage position. I described the interruption positively, as a radial opening the carriage passes through, rather than writing a negative ban on linework.

I did not give the FIG. 1 opening the numeral 38. That numeral belongs to the radial guide as sectioned in FIG. 3; naming it again on the plan view would claim FIG. 1 shows the guide's full form, which the plan view cannot. The opening is described generically, so the two sheets agree without either overstating what it shows.

FIG. 4 needed the same correction because it repeated the gap at the same joint, and its schematic list flagged 'the gap width' as a convention. Leaving that phrase would have kept a flag pointing at geometry that no longer exists and would have re-licensed the depiction the FIG. 6 fix removed. I changed the one sentence and the one list entry and left the wedge, drive face, spring stack, and indicator pin description untouched, since the reviewer confirmed the kinematic directions across FIGS. 1, 2, and 4 already agree.

Nothing in draft/ changed. The reviewer's source ledger passed on the whole text, and both defects had fixes available in the briefs, so widening the description or adding an embodiment to justify a rendering choice would have been the wrong repair. The claims, the numeral table, and the Brief Description of the Drawings were already consistent with the corrected briefs and were left alone.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary, the other the outer. The three are evenly spaced and identically formed, so turning the ring a third of a turn carries each onto the next and all three tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge runs between two points of that boundary lying near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, its pivot mounting, outline, opening and the short arm by which it acts on the stack, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. The bodies meet at a parting line, and at that line the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right and runs up and to the right through an opening left where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position. From that pivot to its outer end it is one straight bar of even width, its two long edges straight and parallel, its outer end closed square across the bar. A separate short arm on the same pivot reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular opening passes through that block from its left face to its right face; apart from that opening the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the opening and below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary, the other the outer. The three are alike in form and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching and the two segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the curvature of the upright edges, and the form of the meeting surfaces.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the parting line in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

An unhatched block lies in each channel and extends to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block held in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block held in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line between the two frame halves the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. # FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching and the two segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the curvature of the upright edges, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the frame material shown radially outside each channel, the frame-wall interruption of FIG. 4 lying outside the fragment shown here.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the parting line in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

An unhatched block lies in each channel and extends to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block held in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block held in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line between the two frame halves the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 18 annular guide: target the wall of the channel holding the block in the upper body.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper unhatched block.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, its pivot mounting, outline, opening and the manner in which it acts on the force-limiting spring stack 54, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. The bodies meet at a parting line, and at that line the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so that the stack lies between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52; the manner of that connection is shown schematically.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right and runs up and to the right through an opening left where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position. From that pivot to its outer end it is one straight bar of even width, its two long edges straight and parallel, its outer end closed square across the bar.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall.

One minor finding, fixed with a single sentence in the FIG. 4 brief.

The fixed edge of the latch housing is recited in claims 2, 11, and 14 and is the datum the description tells the operator to read the indicator pin 56 against, but FIG. 4, the only sheet showing the latch housing 58 and the pin, never identified which surface that is. The brief now has the pin project beyond the outer surface of the top wall and identifies that outer surface as the fixed edge against which the pin's position is read. The disclosure supplies the feature directly ("A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range"), so this identifies an already-drawn surface rather than adding structure.

The edge takes no reference numeral, since neither the numeral table nor the description assigns it one, and the existing target for numeral 56 (the pin above the top wall) already reads on the corrected geometry. Claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings, the numeral table, and every other figure brief are unchanged. FIG. 4 still lists seven numerals and stays inside the brief length limit.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

All three findings are fixed, with the two text edits kept to the exact wording that removes the untraced assertion.

- **FIG. 6 vs FIG. 4**: FIG. 6's fragment is now bounded radially outward by an irregular break line short of the frame's outer wall, rather than by that wall itself. The sheet still shows hatched frame material on both sides of each channel, which is what it exists to show, but it no longer asserts an intact outer wall at the location FIG. 4 shows interrupted to expose the ring drive face 36. The schematic list records the break instead of the disclaimer that could not hold, and the channel sentence now reads against the break line at the right rather than a body edge.
- **Description "radially outside"**: the mounting boss 70 now "stands outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18". That matches the disclosure's "outside the annular guide" and the neutral wording already in claims 8 and 10 and the Summary. The radial placement survives only as a depiction choice in the FIG. 5 brief, and that brief now flags the placement itself as schematic, not merely the block's rectangular outline.
- **FIG. 5's plane**: the Brief Description, the Detailed Description, and the FIG. 5 brief now all say the plane contains the axis of the frame and corresponds in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, passing through the mounting boss. FIG. 5 no longer reads as a section on line 3-3, which would have had to cut the jaw carriage 30, follower 32, radial guide 38, and jaw pad 40 that it does not show, and no cutting-plane designation is owed since the boss appears in no other view.

Claims, the numeral table, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.

input.summary: Fixed all three findings. FIG. 6's fragment is now bounded radially outward by an irregular break line short of the frame's outer wall, so it no longer assigns an intact outer wall to the location FIG. 4 shows interrupted at the ring drive face 36, while keeping the hatched frame material on both sides of each channel that shows the annular guide 18 retaining each segment. The Detailed Description no longer says the mounting boss 70 stands radially outside the annular guide 18; it now says outside, matching the disclosure and the neutral wording already in claims 8 and 10, with the radial placement left as a declared depiction choice in the FIG. 5 brief. The FIG. 5 plane is now described identically in the Brief Description, the Detailed Description and the FIG. 5 brief as containing the axis of the frame, corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, and passing through the mounting boss. Claims, numeral table, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.
reasoning: For the FIG. 4 and FIG. 6 conflict I bounded the fragment rather than altering structure in either sheet. Both depictions are needed: FIG. 4 must expose the ring drive face 36 for the wedge, and FIG. 6 must show frame material on both sides of each channel to make the retention relationship visible. The break line says only that FIG. 6 stops short of the outer wall, which is a statement about the extent of the view, so neither the interruption nor its absence is asserted at the joint and no arc position for the opening had to be invented.

The channel sentence had to move with the boundary. It read that each channel is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, and the right edge is no longer a body edge, so it now reads against the break line at the right. Without that the brief would have described frame material bounded by an edge the view no longer contains.

On the mounting boss I removed the direction from the description rather than adding source for it. The inventor says only that the boss lies outside the annular guide, and the claims and Summary were already neutral, so the description was the single place asserting a radial relationship plus an intervening outer guide wall. Dropping 'radially' and the consequential clause about the wall leaves the disclosed relationship intact, that the boss is outside the guide and no part of it reaches in, which is what keeps the equipment off the drive path.

I did strengthen one line of the FIG. 5 brief beyond the suggested fix, because the finding rests on the radial placement being a declared convention there and only the block's rectangular outline was actually flagged. The brief now flags the placement radially outside the groove as schematic too, so the convention is confined to the drawing and cannot be read back as an embodiment.

The FIG. 5 plane wording was a cross-reference defect, not new matter. A section on line 3-3 would necessarily cut the jaw carriage 30, follower 32, radial guide 38 and jaw pad 40, none of which FIG. 5 shows, so 'corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3' read as the identical plane. Saying the plane contains the frame axis and corresponds in orientation preserves the reader's orientation cue while locating FIG. 5 at the boss. No cutting-plane designation is owed, since the boss appears in no other view and there is nothing to draw the line on.

I changed the phrase in all three loci at once. Leaving the Brief Description or the FIG. 5 brief on the old wording would have left the drawing description and the figure brief describing different planes, which is the kind of split the numeral and figure synchronization check reads as a defect.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary, the other the outer. The three are alike in form and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge leaves that boundary at a point spaced from the joint and runs toward the joint, slanting steadily inward so that its end nearer the joint lies radially inside the boundary, cutting a little material from the segment, the edge being inclined to the radial direction at that position in the same sense as the face on which the wedge bears in FIG. 4. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.

- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.

The one finding is fixed in the FIG. 2 brief.

Numeral 36 had been specified two ways. FIG. 2 described the ring drive face 36 as a straight edge running between two points of the segment's outer circular boundary, which is a chord: its normal points radially outward at the middle, so a wedge advancing onto it would push the ring radially and not turn it, defeating the function the description assigns the face ("it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially"). That wording was also self-defeating inside FIG. 2, since a line between two points of one circle cannot slant inward toward the joint the whole way. FIG. 4's monotonic ramp is the source-faithful form, the disclosure supporting an inclined drive face that the wedge turns the ring against.

FIG. 2 now describes the same ramp: the edge leaves the outer boundary at a point spaced from the joint and slants steadily inward so its end nearer the joint lies radially inside that boundary, inclined to the radial direction in the same sense as the face the wedge bears on in FIG. 4. That agrees with FIG. 4's "slanting down to the right" at the end nearest the joint, with radially outward toward the top, and with the wedge's downward advance driving the band left.

FIG. 4, the detailed description, the claims, the numeral table, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.

input.summary: Fixed the one reported finding with a single sentence change in figures/FIG-2.md. The ring drive face 36 is no longer described there as a chord between two points of the segment's outer circular boundary; it is now the same monotonic ramp FIG. 4 shows, leaving the outer boundary at a point spaced from the latch joint and slanting steadily inward so that its end nearer the joint lies radially inside that boundary, inclined to the radial direction in the same sense as the face the wedge bears on in FIG. 4. That removes the conflict between the two briefs and matches the function the description assigns the face. FIG. 4, the detailed description, the claims, the numeral table, and every other figure brief are unchanged.
reasoning: The two briefs specified one numbered feature two incompatible ways, and only one of them can do the work the description assigns it. A chord's normal is radially outward at its middle, so a wedge advancing onto it delivers no circumferential component and the coupled ring does not turn. FIG. 4's ramp, whose radius decreases steadily toward the latch joint, is what produces the stated result that the wedge's advance drives the band circumferentially, so FIG. 2 was the sheet to correct and FIG. 4 was left alone.

The correction is source-faithful rather than a drawing accommodation. The disclosure says closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke, which affirmatively requires a face inclined to the wedge's advance; the description already states that inclination in the same words. So the ramp was supported before this turn and needed no new text, and I added none.

I tied the FIG. 2 wording to FIG. 4 by sense rather than by angle. Saying the edge is inclined to the radial direction in the same sense as the face the wedge bears on in FIG. 4 fixes the handedness the two views must share without inventing a degree value, a ramp length, or a start point that no inventor passage gives.

I did not add the face's form or inclination to the schematic list. Flagging it schematic would say the inclination is a depiction choice, when it is the disclosed feature that converts wedge advance into ring rotation. The list still covers only what is genuinely a rendering choice there: which segment carries the face, its position on the outer boundary, and its length.

I checked the handedness against the neighbouring views before writing it. In FIG. 4 the left band is segment 24 with radially outward up and the joint toward its right, so a surface slanting down to the right is one whose radius falls toward the joint, which is exactly what the new FIG. 2 sentence describes; and that rotation sense still carries each follower toward the inner end of its slot as the slots are tilted in FIG. 2, so the jaws advance inward.
