Claim 1 still turns on the segmented cam ring coupled by closure at complementary faces at both the hinge end and the latch end so that it rotates in the annular guide as one ring through a limited stroke, with the three followers in oblique slots advancing the carriages in synchronism and the force-limiting spring stack in the latch-handle-to-wedge drive train. The wedge-on-ring-drive-face clause already recited the inclination that the corrected figure now depicts, so the fix brought the drawing into line with the claim rather than the reverse.

The one finding is fixed in all three loci, and FIG. 1 was left untouched.

FIG. 5 was styled as a sectional view taken on a plane while no cutting plane for it appeared on any other view, unlike FIG. 3, which is anchored by the designated line 3-3 in FIG. 1. The cause is that the mounting boss 70 is optional and deliberately absent from FIG. 1, so there is no view to cut it from. Adding the boss and a section line to FIG. 1 would have required inventing a circumferential location for it, which the disclosure does not supply, so the repair was to the caption rather than to the drawing set.

FIG. 5 is now a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, worded consistently in the Brief Description of the Drawings, the Detailed Description, and the FIG. 5 brief. That form needs no designated cutting plane. The orientation cross-reference to FIG. 3 is kept, since it is what tells the reader how to read the annular guide 18 and the segmented cam ring 20 in that view, and the plane is still stated to pass through the mounting boss 70 in the description.

FIG. 3 remains the only view designated by a section line, and line 3-3 still agrees across the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 3 brief, the Brief Description, and the Detailed Description. Claims, the numeral table, and every other figure brief are unchanged.

It is now an enlarged fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, rather than a sectional view taken on a plane, so it no longer owes a cutting-plane indication on another view. The wording matches across draft/07-drawings.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md, and figures/FIG-5.md. FIG. 1 was not touched, no cutting-plane line was added, and no circumferential location for the mounting boss was invented. Claims, numeral table, and every other figure brief are unchanged.
reasoning: The defect was a caption-style mismatch between two same-styled views, not a missing drawing. FIG. 3 is anchored by the designated line 3-3 drawn in FIG. 1, while FIG. 5 was captioned the same way with nothing to anchor it. Restyling it as a fragmentary view with parts shown in section removes the obligation, because that form of view is not cut from a designated plane.

I fixed the caption rather than the drawing set because the alternative would have manufactured source. The mounting boss 70 is optional and absent from FIG. 1, so adding it there together with a section line would have required choosing a circumferential position for the boss around the frame. The inventor says only that the frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide, so any such position would be untraced matter added to serve a formality.

I kept the orientation cross-reference to FIG. 3 rather than dropping it with the section styling. It is not a cutting-plane designation; it is what tells the reader that FIG. 5 is read with radially outward toward the top and the axis running left to right, which is how the annular guide 18 and the segmented cam ring 20 in that view are understood. Removing it would have cost the reader the orientation while gaining nothing.

The description keeps the statement that the plane passes through the mounting boss 70. That locates the cut relative to the boss, which is the part FIG. 5 exists to show, without asserting where the boss sits on the frame.

I changed all three loci in one pass. Leaving the Brief Description or the FIG. 5 brief on the old sectional-view wording would have left the drawing description and the figure brief disagreeing about the character of the same view, which is the kind of split the synchronization check reports.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed, in the FIG. 4 brief and the one description sentence that listed its parts.

**Coupling faces at the latch end.** FIG. 4 shows the clamped, over-center state, and in that state its own drive geometry has opened the latch-end joint: the wedge drives the left band away from the parting line through the whole ring stroke, and abutting complementary faces can push but not pull, so the load path runs around through the hinge-end joint. The brief now has the band ends face one another across the parting line along complementary surfaces, rather than asserting contact there. FIG. 6 is untouched, since it shows the frame halves closed rather than clamped, which is the state in which those faces do meet.

**Numeral 20 on an individual segment.** FIG. 4 draws the two segments as distinct bands at the same joint FIG. 6 shows, so the assembly numeral was landing on a body that FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 number 24. The left band is now the second cam ring segment 24, which is consistent with FIG. 2 placing the ring drive face 36 on segment 24, and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The numeral list carries 22 and 24 in place of 20, putting the sheet at eight numerals, and the passing mention of the ring in the schematic list now names it without a numeral so no numeral appears in the brief that the sheet does not label. The Detailed Description's FIG. 4 sentence now names segments 22 and 24, keeping its part list identical to the sheet's.

Numeral 20 stays correct in FIGS. 2, 3, and 5, where the ring is shown whole, and in the description's shape-neutral statements about the coupled ring. Claims, the numeral table, `draft/07-drawings.md`, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.

input.summary: Fixed both findings. In figures/FIG-4.md the latch-end band ends now face one another across the parting line along complementary surfaces instead of being drawn in contact, which matches the clamped over-center state that sheet depicts and in which the wedge has driven the left band away from the joint. Also in FIG-4.md the two bands are now numbered as segments rather than as the assembly: the left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22, the numeral list carries 22 and 24 in place of 20, and the schematic list names the segmented cam ring without a numeral. The Detailed Description sentence introducing FIG. 4 now names segments 22 and 24 so its part list still matches the sheet exactly. FIG. 6, the claims, the numeral table, draft/07-drawings.md and the other figure briefs are unchanged.
reasoning: The contact assertion failed against FIG. 4's own kinematics. That sheet fixes the clamped, over-center state, and its wedge drives the left band away from the parting line through the whole ring stroke; abutting complementary faces transmit push and not pull, so in the clamped state the load runs around through the hinge-end joint and the latch-end faces stand apart. Since the stroke has to carry the jaws across a range of pipe diameters and this is an enlarged view, the separation is not a hairline. Saying the ends face one another along complementary surfaces keeps the joint identifiable without instructing the renderer to close a gap the drive has opened.

I did not touch FIG. 6, because the two sheets show different states. FIG. 6 depicts the frame halves closed, which is exactly when closure has brought the faces together and before the latch drives the ring, so contact is correct there. Changing it to match FIG. 4 would have destroyed the one view that shows the coupling the invention turns on.

The description needed no change for that finding. Its statement that the faces are each shaped so one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint is shape-neutral and source-supported, and it does not assert contact in any particular state, so the defect lived entirely in the brief.

On the numeral, FIG. 4 draws the same joint as FIG. 6 with the two segments as separate bands, so an assembly numeral on one band conflicts with the segment numerals the other briefs use for the same bodies. The identification is forced rather than chosen: FIG. 2 puts the ring drive face 36 on segment 24, FIG. 4 puts that face on its left band, so the left band is segment 24 and the right band is segment 22.

Two consequential edits kept the sheet self-consistent. The numeral list now carries 22 and 24 instead of 20, which brings FIG. 4 to eight numerals, at the per-sheet limit but within it; and the schematic list's passing reference to the segmented cam ring 20 dropped its numeral, so the brief no longer names a numeral that the sheet does not label. Numeral 20 remains right in FIGS. 2, 3 and 5, where the ring appears whole and no joint is shown.

I updated the description's FIG. 4 sentence for the same reason the numeral moved: it enumerated the parts that figure shows, and leaving 20 there would have told the reader to look for a callout the sheet no longer carries. draft/07-drawings.md needed nothing, since it names the segmented cam ring in words without a numeral.

Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs; no application text changed.

**FIG. 2's cross-figure sense clause.** The sentence already fixed the ring drive face 36 completely in FIG. 2's own coordinates: the edge leaves the outer boundary at a point spaced from the joint and slants steadily inward so its end nearer the joint lies radially inside that boundary. The appended reference to "the same sense as the face ... in FIG. 4" pointed at the opposite-hand view, where the same surface reads mirrored on the page, so it instructed the reverse of the incline the sentence had just specified. The clause is deleted and the sentence ends at its own geometry. FIG. 4 still fixes the identical surface independently in its coordinates, and the two now agree.

**FIG. 1's lever attitude.** FIG. 1 gave the renderer no direction for the latch lever while FIG. 4 fixes it precisely, for one part in one state, so FIG. 1 could have been drawn with the lever swung the other way about the latch. It now extends radially outward and inclines toward the first frame half 10, which is what FIG. 4's "up and to the right, leaning past upright" maps to when read from FIG. 1's opposite axial side, and only the lever's form and proportions remain schematic.

I referred to the latch handle by name rather than by numeral 50 in the FIG. 1 brief. FIG. 1 does not label that part and its numeral list is already at eight, so citing the numeral there would have named a callout the sheet does not carry.

The claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings, numeral table, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.

43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
44	
45	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

content.content:
1	A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.
2	
3	In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.
4	
5	Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.
6	
7	In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.
8	
9	In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.
10	
11	In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.
12

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

The one finding is fixed in the Detailed Description.

The description had defined the latch 16 as including the wedge 52 among its components, while claim 1, claim 10, and the Summary all recite the wedge as a separate element moved by the latch, and the disclosure treats it the same way ("Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring"). The sentence now reads: "The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end and a latch handle 50, and moves a wedge 52 through a drive train that includes a force-limiting spring stack 54 between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52." That also introduces the drive train with an indefinite article, curing the definite reference to a drive train that had not yet been mentioned.

One further sentence in the same specification carried the same membership implication: the paragraph on the ring drive face 36 spoke of "the wedge of the latch", which now reads "the wedge moved by the latch". Without that, "the latch" would still have read on two different collections of parts in one document. The rest of the section and the Operation section already describe the wedge only as advanced and retracted by movement of the latch handle 50, and the FIG. 4 brief treats it as a separate block in the cavity, so nothing else moved.

The claims, Summary, abstract, numeral table, and every figure brief are unchanged.

input.summary: Fixed the reported inconsistency in draft/08-detailed-description.md. The latch 16 no longer includes the wedge 52 among its components; it comprises a latch housing 58 and a latch handle 50 and moves a wedge 52 through a drive train that includes the force-limiting spring stack 54 between the handle and the wedge, matching claim 1, claim 10, the Summary and the disclosure. The same paragraph now introduces the drive train with an indefinite article. I also changed one later phrase in the same file, 'the wedge of the latch', to 'the wedge moved by the latch', because it carried the identical membership implication and would have left 'the latch' reading on two different collections of parts. Claims, Summary, abstract, numeral table and all figure briefs are unchanged.
reasoning: The claims and the source both put the wedge outside the latch, so the description was the item to correct. Claim 1 recites a wedge movable by the latch as a distinct element and then defines the latch as comprising a latch handle and the spring stack; claim 2 adds only the housing and indicator pin; and the disclosure says closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring. Rewriting the claims to match the description would have changed what 'the latch' covers, which is scope, so the fix went the other way.

I extended the fix by one phrase beyond the finding. The ring drive face paragraph said the face sits where 'the wedge of the latch' can reach, which is the same possessive membership the finding is about. Leaving it would have meant the corrected sentence and an earlier sentence still described different collections of parts, so the defect would recur on the next read; it now says the wedge moved by the latch, which is claim 1's own relationship.

The article change came with the same sentence rather than as a separate edit. The old wording referred to 'the drive train' before any drive train had been mentioned in the description; the replacement introduces 'a drive train' at first use, so the later references in the spring stack paragraph, which speak of the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52, now have an antecedent.

I checked the rest of the specification before stopping. The two-positions paragraph, the spring stack paragraph and the Operation section already describe the wedge only as advanced and retracted by movement of the latch handle 50, and the FIG. 4 brief draws it as a separate block in the cavity, so no other text or brief asserted the wedge to be part of the latch and nothing else needed touching.
